## Human reinforcement: new technicians for sustainable management

The selection process convened by the Motril City Council has concluded with the incorporation of new workers into the team that manages the Charca de Suárez. This is a staff expansion that responds to evidence confirmed over recent years: the complexity of maintaining an artificial wetland in ecological balance has far exceeded the capacities of the original team. Municipal sources confirm the arrival of between two and three technicians, who join an already consolidated structure where biologists, environmental educators, and maintenance workers coexist.

The decision is neither an administrative whim nor a concession to the natural growth of the workforce. It responds to an operational need that has become increasingly apparent as the Charca has gained relevance as a protected natural area and as a visitor destination. Every spring, the wetland becomes a hive of reproductive activity that requires constant monitoring. Every autumn, the first rains force precise adjustments to water levels to favor the arrival of wintering birds. And throughout the year, the pressure of invasive species demands vigilance that allows no pauses.

Among the functions assigned to the new technicians is the control of water levels, a task that may seem mechanical but actually holds considerable complexity. The Charca de Suárez is not a natural wetland that self-regulates, but rather an artificial system that depends on freshwater inputs and careful management of gates and internal channels. A calculation error in water volume can alter the salinity of the lagoons, modify marsh vegetation, or leave species that depend on shallow water surfaces for feeding without suitable habitat. The new technicians are incorporated precisely to reinforce this vigilance and ensure that water cycles adjust to the needs of the fauna in each season.

Another of the responsibilities assumed by the newcomers is the eradication of invasive species, with the common reed as the main enemy to combat. This plant, native to Asia and widely spread throughout the entire Mediterranean basin, has an extraordinary colonization capacity that suffocates native vegetation and reduces the diversity of habitats available for birds. In the Charca de Suárez, the reed has required periodic interventions that combine mechanical clearing with specific treatments to prevent regrowth. The incorporation of personnel allows these campaigns to be intensified and extended to areas of the wetland that until now received less frequent attention.

Nest monitoring constitutes the third pillar of the new incorporations. During spring, the Charca hosts breeding colonies of species as sensitive as the purple heron, the little bittern, or the purple swamphen, whose presence has been one of the great successes of the management of the space. Nest monitoring allows early detection of predation problems, human disturbances, or habitat alterations that could compromise breeding success. It is silent work, carried out with binoculars and field notebooks, but it is essential for evaluating the health of the ecosystem and making management decisions based on real data.

Visitor attention completes the range of functions assumed by the new technicians. The opening of the Interpretation Center has notably increased the number of people who come to the Charca, and with them has also grown the demand for information, guided visits, and educational activities. The environmental educators who were already part of the team needed reinforcements to attend to school groups, associations, and tourists without neglecting conservation tasks. The new workers integrate into this dynamic with a versatile profile that allows them to alternate between public attention and field tasks.

The expansion of the workforce also reflects a change in the philosophy of managing the space. For years, the Charca de Suárez operated with a reduced team that compensated for the lack of resources with admirable dedication. The growth of the wetland, both in managed surface area and ecological complexity, has made that model unsustainable. The incorporation of new technicians represents an implicit recognition that biodiversity conservation cannot depend on voluntarism or the goodwill of a few. It requires stable structures, qualified personnel, and long-term planning that allows anticipating problems rather than reacting once they have already manifested.

The Motril City Council has not detailed the economic cost of these incorporations, but it has made clear that they are part of the global investment strategy in the wetland that exceeds one and a half million euros over the last four years. The commitment to human capital is consistent with the investment in infrastructure: it is useless to build a modern interpretation center or condition trails if there is not enough personnel to maintain the ecosystem that gives meaning to everything else. The new technicians are, in this sense, the missing piece to complete a mechanism that aspires to consolidate the Charca de Suárez as a reference for sustainable wetland management on the Andalusian coast.

The resulting workforce combines scientific, outreach, and operational profiles that complement each other. Biologists provide the technical knowledge necessary to interpret changes in vegetation or bird populations. Environmental educators translate that knowledge into accessible language for the public. Maintenance workers execute the physical interventions required by the wetland, from repairing gates to cleaning channels. The new technicians insert themselves into this structure with cross-cutting functions that reinforce each of the work areas.

The upcoming declaration of the Charca as a Special Protection Area for Birds adds another argument in favor of this staff reinforcement. The European protection status implies monitoring and conservation obligations that require adequate technical and administrative capacity. The Motril City Council is getting ahead of those requirements with a workforce sized to assume the responsibilities entailed by the management of a space integrated into the Natura 2000 Network. The incorporation of the new workers is not, therefore, an arrival point, but a starting point for a stage in which the Charca de Suárez must demonstrate that it can combine strict conservation with public use and environmental education.
